analysis.title: Weekly Commentary: Value Breakout Shows Benefits of Diversification
key_insights: Last week saw a sharp rotation out of growth and into value. The Russell Value Index and S&P Value Index both hit all-time highs while the Nasdaq had one of its largest recent selloffs.

Siegel compares the divergence to 2000, when value rose toward new highs after the Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and fell roughly 60% over the next year. He does not believe today resembles the 2000 technology bubble.

The rotation is driven by uncertainty over the scale and durability of the AI investment boom. Data-center construction and AI capital spending have created large demand for funds and pushed real interest rates higher.
The 10-year Treasury yield moved back below 5%, supporting bonds and rate-sensitive value stocks.

Siegel treats bonds and value stocks as natural hedges against the dominant AI trade. If AI investment accelerates, growth benefits while bonds and many value stocks face higher real rates. If AI demand or returns are questioned, long-term rates fall and value outperforms.
He attributes the move in long-term rates to real rates, not to worsening inflation expectations or mainly the federal deficit. Long-term inflation expectations have been edging lower.
If the AI buildout slows, the effect extends beyond tech: less data-center financing demand, slower economic activity, less inflation pressure and meaningfully lower interest rates.

This week's Fed meeting should be uneventful, with no Summary of Economic Projections or dot plot and no policy change expected. December is the more interesting meeting, with markets still pricing the possibility of another rate increase.
Trade data is the final major input to third-quarter GDP. Current forecasts cluster around 3% growth.
No decisive AI-driven productivity acceleration has appeared in the aggregate statistics, which Siegel calls one of the most important missing pieces of the AI story.
Oil prices remain elevated, but gasoline prices have behaved better as refining spreads narrowed.
Siegel sees potential movement toward a Russia-Ukraine settlement and much less evidence of an imminent breakthrough involving Iran.
Investors who own only AI winners carry more concentrated macroeconomic risk than they may realize. Diversification can work when the market narrative changes.
